text: The structural divergence across US banking institutions is overwhelmingly driven by a single primary causal mechanism: **balance-sheet scale and capital-markets integration capacity**. Institutions possessing diversified global markets, robust investment banking franchises, and immense asset scale (such as JPMorgan Chase & Co. and Morgan Stanley) have leveraged trading and fee cycles to achieve extraordinary revenue acceleration, exemplified by JPM's +27.7% year-over-year revenue growth to $57.347B [E01, E02] and MS's +27.1% growth to $21.348B [E28, E29]. Conversely, regional and mid-cap banks constrained by traditional lending models and deposit cost pressures exhibit flat to contracting operating revenues, such as Bank of America (-3.0%) [E05], KeyCorp (-2.3%) [E17], and Regions Financial (-2.0%) [E23]. This stark division proves that scale and fee-income diversification insulate money-center giants from net-interest margin compression, whereas pure-play lenders remain vulnerable to interest rate cycles and deposit beta adjustments. This framework would be decisively falsified if regional banking institutions with smaller asset bases and limited capital markets operations consistently outperform money-center institutions in organic revenue growth during periods of monetary tightening.
cause_effect_dynamics: D1: Large-scale asset bases and diversified non-interest fee streams drive outsized revenue growth in money-center banks because capital markets activity and trading volume disproportionately benefit institutions with global market access (E01, E02, E28, E29).

D2: Traditional regional lenders experience top-line contraction or stagnation because their reliance on net interest income leaves them acutely exposed to deposit cost pressures and yield curve repricing without offsetting investment banking fees (E05, E17, E23).

D3: Regulatory constraints and asset caps restrict balance-sheet expansion, capping organic loan growth and interest income despite broader macroeconomic tailwinds for well-capitalized domestic institutions (E07, E08, E09).
